papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: The Jiegeng Decoction (JGD) is a classic traditional Chinese medicinal formulation that consists of Platycodon grandiflorus (Jacq.) A. DC. and Glycyrrhiza uralensis Fisch. This formulation was first recorded in the "Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases" during the Eastern Han Dynasty. Clinically, JGD has been employed as a fundamental prescription in the clinical management of various pulmonary disorders. Unlike previous studies, which focused primarily on the addition and subtraction prescriptions derived from JGD, the present study first sought to investigate the associated mechanisms and identify the principal bioactive metabolites of this foundational prescription for the treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-like pulmonary injury, with particular attention to its underexplored effects on the intestine. METHODS: A cigarette smoke/lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced rat model of COPD-like pulmonary injury was used to assess the effects of JGD on pulmonary and intestinal injury. This assessment utilized histological staining, immunofluorescence, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. To explore and validate the underlying mechanisms and bioactive metabolites, lung transcriptomics, untargeted metabolomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, UPLC‒Q‒Orbitrap‒MS/MS, and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages were utilized. RESULTS: An animal study revealed that JGD mitigated pulmonary histopathological damage, mucus hypersecretion, and the release of inflammatory cytokines in rats exposed to cigarette smoke/LPS-. Comprehensive transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses suggested that JGD may ameliorate inflammatory responses by modulating arachidonic acid metabolism, potentially through the upregulation of PPARγ expressions. Additionally, JGD alleviated intestinal injury and inflammation, restored the expressions of the barrier-associated proteins MUC2 and ZO-1, and was associated with alterations in the composition of the gut microbiota. Notably, specific microbial taxa were significantly correlated with pathological indicators and arachidonic acid metabolites. A total of 156 JGD-derived metabolites were detected and annotated in JGD, 77 of which were absorbed into the bloodstream. Among these compounds, liquiritigenin (LG) has emerged as a potential bioactive metabolite that can interact with PPARγ. In vitro studies demonstrated that both JGD and LG mitigated LPS-induced inflammation in RAW264.7 cells by restoring PPARγ expressions. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of PPARγ using GW9662 significantly reduced these protective effects, supporting the involvement of PPARγ signaling in LG-mediated inflammatory regulation. CONCLUSION: JGD may mitigate COPD-like pulmonary injury through a multitarget approach associated with the upregulation of PPARγ expressions, the modulation of arachidonic acid metabolism, the restoration of intestinal barrier-associated protein expression, and changes in the gut microbial composition. The LG within JGD may serve as a bioactive metabolite that contributes to these therapeutic effects.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Dysregulation of the pulmonary endothelial barrier precipitates the edema and inflammation central to sepsis-associated acute lung injury (ALI). Although the G-protein-coupled receptor GPR84 orchestrates various inflammatory responses, its specific contribution to maintaining microvascular integrity during sepsis remains largely undefined. METHODS: We explored the therapeutic efficacy of GPR84 inhibition using a cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) mouse model and LPS-challenged lung microvascular endothelial cells (MLMECs). RESULTS: Pulmonary GPR84 expression surged following septic insult, and its pharmacological blockade via selective inhibitors (GLPG1205 or TUG-2181) effectively mitigated alveolar damage. This intervention restored respiratory mechanics-including peak expiratory flow (PEF) and airway resistance (Raw)-and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine concentrations (TNF-α, IL-6, CXCL15) within the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Furthermore, GPR84 inhibition curtailed vascular protein leakage and preserved Occludin expression across both experimental models. At the molecular level, GPR84 signaling appeared to facilitate the LPS-induced upregulation of the transcription factor YY1. In cultured endothelial cells, the barrier-protective effect of GPR84 inhibition was diminished by YY1 overexpression, indicating a functional role for YY1 in this in vitro system. DISCUSSION: Collectively, these results suggest that GPR84 inhibition attenuates sepsis-associated ALI in association with YY1 suppression in vivo, identifying GPR84 as a candidate therapeutic target warranting further preclinical and clinical evaluation.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Africa seemed to have had low SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 morbidity and mortality. While several studies reported high SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity among healthy Africans, others hypothesized that this could have resulted from pre-existing cross-reactive antibodies. Our study tracks trends in seropositivity across three West African countries during the Delta- and Omicron-dominant pandemic periods using validated SARS-CoV-2 IgG/IgM rapid diagnostic tests (Prestige Diagnostics in Ghana and Burkina Faso; SD Biosensor in Nigeria). METHODS: Cross-sectional studies were conducted in three West African countries (Burkina Faso, Ghana, and Nigeria), with study sites conveniently selected within each country. Using validated immunoassay kits with published validation procedures, SARS-CoV-2 antibodies were detected in peripheral blood during the Delta- and Omicron-dominant periods. Because we did not perform widespread viral sequencing on participant samples, we could not attribute seropositivity to a specific variant; instead, we classified sampling periods by the variant reported as dominant nationally/globally at the time of sample collection. Participants' demographic and clinical data were obtained using a semi-structured questionnaire, and the primary outcome was the proportion of each population with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies. RESULTS: Across the 3 countries, 20,748 participants were recruited, and SARS-CoV-2 IgG seropositivity ranged from 24.1 to 76.4%, with higher rates during the Omicron-dominant period. All sites showed low self-reported vaccination rates, suggesting that seropositivity may be primarily driven by natural infection rather than vaccination. While there was a significant positive association between seropositivity and age across all sites, the association with other demographic factors was country-dependent, and most participants expressed positive opinions of vaccination. CONCLUSION: This is one of the largest multi-country community-based SARS-CoV-2 seroepidemiology studies in Africa, showing widespread exposure to SARS-CoV-2 infection among our study population across three West African countries. These findings are consistent with a marked disconnect between high population exposure and low reported clinical burden, underscoring the need for strengthened community surveillance.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection in the host and subsequent treatment with anti-tuberculosis drugs impact lung pathophysiology and influence the lung and gut microbiome. Elucidating the role of the gut microbiome and its metabolites in the perturbed metabolic and immune functions observed in tuberculosis (TB) might help design corrective prebiotic and probiotic mixtures. METHODOLOGY: In this study, fecal samples (n = 107) of drug-naïve active TB patients (ATB) and controls (other respiratory disease: NTB and healthy) from the two clinical sites were analyzed for microbiota composition (16S rRNA sequencing), metabolites (GC-TOF-MS), and their correlation. In addition, a longitudinal follow-up study was conducted to understand the dynamics of the microbiota and metabolites during anti-TB treatment in a small cohort (n = 10). RESULTS: Gut microbiota showed site-specificity; however, an overall reduction in alpha diversity was observed in disease states compared with healthy subjects. Underrepresentation of gut commensals (Faecalibacterium, Ligilactobacillus and Romboustia) and overrepresentation of Thomasclavelia and Clostridioides were observed among active TB patients. The longitudinally followed-up ATB subjects undergoing treatment showed a time-dependent increase in beta-diversity variance. Over time, the beta diversity of follow-up subjects was almost similar to that of healthy controls. Decrease in the abundance of Streptococcus occurred after anti-TB treatment, with higher levels of opportunistic pathogens, such as Escherichia and Stenotrophomonas. Similarly, specific fecal metabolites also returned to pretreatment levels in relative abundance at later time points. CONCLUSIONS: The gut microbiota of TB patients showed dysbiosis at the time of case presentation and partially resolved upon complete therapeutic interventions. Partial recovery of microbiota observed during treatment is also reflected in the fecal metabolome, indicating the possible use of microbiome and metabolites as adjunct therapeutics in TB.

papers.abstract_en: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is characterized by dysregulated pulmonary immune responses, and effective targeted therapeutic strategies remain an unmet clinical need. Accumulating preclinical and clinical correlative data reveal complex interconnections between gut microbiota and ferroptosis-driven immunopathology in ARDS, yet an integrated mechanistic understanding of the gut-lung pathological axis remains incomplete. This review puts forward a testable conceptual temporal framework for ARDS-related gut-lung crosstalk. Evidence supporting the gut-to-lung limb is comparatively more abundant, whereas the full sequential pathogenic cascade has not been rigorously validated. Gut-derived metabolites remodel pulmonary cell phenotypes, macrophage functional states, neutrophil extracellular trap formation and T-cell homeostasis, potentially sustaining a self-amplifying ferroptosis-inflammatory vicious cycle that may drive pulmonary immunometabolic reprogramming. Targeting this regulatory cascade may yield promising conceptual therapeutic avenues, including microbiota-modulating interventions, anti-ferroptotic strategies and multi-omics-guided precision approaches. Major knowledge gaps persist: most mechanistic observations are extrapolated from non-ARDS animal models; temporally-separated preclinical experiments that induce lung injury prior to gut-targeted manipulation are scarce; and well-controlled human studies disentangling pulmonary-driven effects from ICU confounders are urgently required. This sequence represents an etiology-dependent working model rather than a uniform chronological hierarchy for all ARDS. In direct-pulmonary ARDS, alveolar injury may precede gut dysbiosis; in indirect/sepsis-associated ARDS, systemic inflammation, intestinal hypoperfusion and antibiotic exposure may occur before, or simultaneously with, overt pulmonary ferroptotic injury.

papers.abstract_en: Toluene diisocyanate (TDI) is a major cause of occupational asthma (OA) with few effective therapies. Dysregulated mitophagy signaling and cellular senescence have been implicated in airway inflammation; however, their roles in TDI-induced asthma remain unclear. The natural alkaloid liensinine (Lie) has been reported to inhibit mitophagy, but its protective potential in asthma remains unexplored. This study investigated whether Lie could alleviate experimental asthma by attenuating PINK1-associated mitophagy signaling and the related cellular senescence. We established mouse and cellular models of TDI-induced asthma. In vivo, mice received intraperitoneal Lie and intranasal adeno-associated virus (AAV) for PINK1 overexpression. In vitro, HBE135-E6E7 cells were exposed to TDI-human serum albumin (TDI-HSA) and transduced with lentivirus for PINK1 overexpression. Lie significantly mitigated airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), inflammation, and fibrosis. Molecular docking predicted a potential interaction between Lie and PINK1. Lie attenuated TDI-induced PINK1-associated mitophagy signaling, restored mitochondrial function, and reduced senescence. PINK1 overexpression largely reversed the protective effects of Lie on mitochondrial function and attenuated its senescence-reducing effect. In a Transwell co-culture system, pretreatment of TDI-HSA-stimulated HBE135-E6E7 cells with Lie was associated with reduced proliferation, migration, and fibrotic marker expression in MRC-5 cells in the lower chamber, possibly through attenuation of TDI-HSA-induced epithelial injury. Lie pretreatment attenuated PINK1-associated mitophagy signaling and the related cellular senescence in a TDI-induced experimental asthma model.

papers.abstract_en: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive and ultimately fatal interstitial lung disease characterized by persistent epithelial injury, immune dysregulation, fibroblast activation, excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition, and irreversible architectural remodeling of the lung. Although currently approved antifibrotic therapies can slow disease progression, their inability to reverse established fibrosis, together with systemic toxicity and limited drug accessibility to fibrotic lesions, continues to restrict therapeutic efficacy. Inhalation-based drug delivery has emerged as a promising approach for improving local drug exposure while minimizing systemic adverse effects. In particular, inhalable nanodelivery systems provide versatile platforms for enhancing pulmonary retention, improving lesion accessibility, and overcoming the biological barriers associated with fibrotic lungs. In this review, the major pathological mechanisms underlying IPF are briefly introduced to provide the biological context for therapeutic intervention. Emphasis is placed on the biological barriers that limit pulmonary drug delivery, including airway mucus, alveolar macrophage clearance, and the dense fibrotic ECM. Recent advances in inhalable nanotherapeutics designed to overcome these barriers are highlighted, including strategies for improving mucus and ECM penetration, remodeling pathological microenvironments, regulating fibrosis-associated signaling networks, and promoting tissue repair. This review adopts a pathology-oriented perspective to illustrate how the pathophysiological features of IPF can guide the rational design of inhalable nanomedicines. Finally, current translational challenges and future opportunities are discussed, providing insights into further development of inhalable therapeutics for more effective control of IPF.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a progressive respiratory disorder driven by immune dysregulation and ferroptosis, with limited therapies addressing its underlying pathogenesis. Maxing Loushi Decoction (MXLS), a modified traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formula, has shown clinical efficacy in COPD, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to explore the therapeutic mechanisms of MXLS in COPD. METHODS: A COPD mouse model was established via cigarette smoke (CS) exposure combined with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) administration. MXLS was intragastrically administered, with dexamethasone (DX) as a positive control. Lung function, histopathological changes, CD4+ T cell subsets, PD-1/PD-L1 expression, and ferroptosis-related indicators were evaluated. In vitro experiments included Th17 polarization induction, CD4+ T cell-MLE-12 cell co-culture, and intervention with anti-PD-1 antibody. RESULTS: MXLS significantly improved lung function, alleviated airway inflammation and alveolar destruction in cigarette smoke- and LPS-induced COPD mice, with efficacy comparable to DX. MXLS downregulated PD-1/PD-L1 expression in lung tissue and CD4+ T cells, restored Th17/Treg balance by reducing Th17 cell frequency and increasing Treg cell proportion, and inhibited ferroptosis by reducing Fe2+ accumulation, restoring GSH/SOD levels, and upregulating ferroptosis-related protective proteins (GPX4, SLC7A11, FTH1). In vitro, MXLS-modulated CD4+ T cells alleviated epithelial cell inflammation and ferroptosis, and combining MXLS with anti-PD-1 antibody enhanced these effects. CONCLUSION: MXLS may exerts therapeutic effects in a cigarette smoke- and LPS-induced COPD model, at least in part through modulation of the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway, concurrently restoring Th17/Treg immune homeostasis and inhibiting ferroptosis. This study provides a scientific basis for MXLS as a potential COPD therapy.
